tasks.title: A Committee Selection
tasks.context: A club has 7 men and 5 women. A committee of 4 people is selected at random from the 12 members.
statements: The total number of possible committees is 792.
There are fewer ways to form a committee with exactly 2 men and 2 women than a committee with exactly 3 men and 1 woman.
The probability that the committee consists of all men is less than 5%.
The probability that the committee contains at least one woman is greater than 90%.
The probability of selecting exactly 2 men and 2 women equals 14/33.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — False

$$
Total committees = \binom{12}{4}
$$

$$
= 495
$$

= 495.

The statement is false. (792 is actually \binom{12}{5}, a different selection size — a tempting but incorrect distractor.)

Statement B — False

$$
Compare \binom{7}{2}\cdot \binom{5}{2} = 210 to \binom{7}{3}\cdot \binom{5}{1} = 175
$$

The statement is false. Since 210 is greater than 175, the 2-2 split is more common, not fewer — the statement has the comparison backwards.

Statement C — False

$$
P(all men) = \binom{7}{4}/\binom{12}{4}
$$

$$
= 35/495
$$

= 7.07%, which is not less than 5%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement D — True

$$
P(at least 1 woman) = 1 − P(all men)
$$

$$
= 1 - 0.0707
$$

= 92.93%, which is greater than 90%.

The statement is true.

Statement E — True

$$
P(2 men, 2 women) = \binom{7}{2}\cdot \binom{5}{2}/\binom{12}{4} = 210/495 = 14/33
$$

210/495 simplifies exactly to 14/33 (dividing numerator and denominator by 15), matching the probability computed in Step 1.

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Set up the total and the key sub-counts, with 7 men and 5 women, choosing 4 of the 12 total members.

tasks.title: A Poker Hand
tasks.context: A standard 52-card deck (13 ranks × 4 suits) is shuffled, and 5 cards are dealt at random to form a hand.
statements: The total number of distinct 5-card hands is 2,598,960.
A full house (three of one rank plus two of another) is more likely than four of a kind.
A flush (all five cards the same suit) is more likely than a full house.
The probability of getting two pair is greater than 5%.
The probability of a flush is more than 8 times the probability of four of a kind.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total 5-card hands = \binom{52}{5}
$$

$$
= 2,598,960
$$

= 2,598,960.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
Compare 13·\binom{4}{3}·12·\binom{4}{2} = 3,744 to 13·48 = 624
$$

Full house has 3,744 hands versus 624 for four of a kind, so a full house is indeed more likely — six times as likely.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
Compare \binom{13}{5}·4 = 5,148 to 13·\binom{4}{3}·12·\binom{4}{2} = 3,744
$$

A flush has 5,148 hands versus 3,744 for a full house, so a flush is more likely, even though both are rare.

The statement is true.

Statement D — False

$$
P(two pair) = \binom{13}{2}\cdot \binom{4}{2}²·11·\binom{4}{1}/\binom{52}{5}
$$

$$
= 123,552/2,598,960
$$

= 4.754%, which is not greater than 5%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement E — True

$$
Compare 5,148/624 = 8.25 to 8
$$

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Count each hand type out of the total \binom{52}{5} = 2,598,960 five-card hands.

tasks.title: Restricted Seating
tasks.context: 7 students (4 boys and 3 girls) are seated at random in a row of 7 chairs.
statements: The total number of possible seating arrangements is 5,040.
The number of arrangements in which all 3 girls sit together (in some order) is 720.
The probability that all 3 girls sit together is exactly 1/7.
The probability that boys and girls alternate along the row (in either starting order) is greater than 5%.
The probability that all 3 girls sit together is more than 5 times the probability of an alternating arrangement.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total arrangements = 7!
$$

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
Arrangements with girls together = 5!·3!
$$

Treating the 3 girls as a single block gives 5 units to arrange (5!), and the girls can be ordered 3! ways within the block: 5!·3! = 720.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
P(girls together) = 5!·3!/7! = 720/5,040 = 1/7
$$

720/5,040 simplifies exactly to 1/7, matching the probability from Step 1.

The statement is true.

Statement D — False

$$
P(alternating) = 4!·3!/7! = 144/5,040 = 1/35
$$

$$
= 144/5,040
$$

= 2.86%, which is not greater than 5%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement E — False

$$
Compare (1/7)/(1/35) = 5 to "more than 5"
$$

The statement is false. This is the same trap as "exactly at the boundary is not beyond the boundary."
tasks.solution_overview: Set up the total arrangements, and the block-method count for keeping the 3 girls together.

tasks.title: Quality Control Sampling
tasks.context: A shipment contains 20 items, of which 4 are defective. An inspector randomly selects 5 items, without replacement, for testing.
statements: The total number of possible samples of 5 items is 15,504.
The probability that the sample contains exactly 2 defective items is greater than 20%.
The probability that the sample contains no defective items is less than 30%.
The probability that the sample contains at least one defective item is less than 70%.
Among the possible counts of defective items in the sample (0 through 4), exactly 1 defective item is the single most likely outcome.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total samples = \binom{20}{5}
$$

$$
= 15,504
$$

= 15,504.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
P(exactly 2 defective) = \binom{4}{2}\cdot \binom{16}{3}/\binom{20}{5}
$$

$$
= 3,360/15,504
$$

= 21.67%, which is greater than 20%.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
P(zero defective) = \binom{16}{5}/\binom{20}{5}
$$

$$
= 4,368/15,504
$$

= 28.17%, which is less than 30%.

The statement is true.

Statement D — False

$$
P(at least 1 defective) = 1 − P(zero defective)
$$

$$
= 1 - 0.2817
$$

= 71.83%, which is not less than 70%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement E — True

$$
Compare P(0), P(1), P(2), P(3), P(4) directly
$$

= 28.17%.

Comparing all five possible counts: P(0) ≈ 28.17%, P(1) ≈ 46.96%, P(2) ≈ 21.67%, P(3) ≈ 3.10%, P(4) ≈ 0.10%.

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the hypergeometric counting method: 20 items total, 4 defective, 16 good, sample size 5.

tasks.title: Rolling the Dice
tasks.context: 5 fair six-sided dice are rolled at once, and the 5 results are recorded in order (each die is distinguishable).
statements: The total number of possible outcomes is 7,776.
The probability that all five dice show different numbers is greater than 20%.
The probability that at least two dice show the same number is less than 80%.
The probability that all five dice show different numbers equals exactly 1/6.
If only 3 dice were rolled instead of 5, the probability of all different values would be lower than with 5 dice.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total outcomes = 6⁵
$$

Each of the 5 dice has 6 possible outcomes, independently, giving 6⁵ = 7,776 total outcomes.

The statement is true.

Statement B — False

$$
P(all different) = 6·5·4·3·2/6⁵
$$

$$
= 5/54
$$

= 9.26%, which is not greater than 20%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement C — False

$$
P(at least two same) = 1 − P(all different)
$$

$$
= 1 - 5
$$

= 95%, which is not less than 80%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true (95%).

Statement D — False

$$
Compare 5/54 to 1/6
$$

$$
= 5/54
$$

= 0.0926.

The statement is false. These are not equal — a common error is to assume each die independently has a 1/6 chance of "being different," but the constraint compounds across all 5 dice.

Statement E — False

$$
Compare P(all different, 3 dice)
$$

$$
= 120/216
$$

= 55.56%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true (55.56%).
tasks.solution_overview: Count outcomes for 5 distinguishable dice, then the sub-case where all five show different numbers.

tasks.title: Find the Missing Value
tasks.context: In a group of n people, every pair of people shakes hands exactly once. The total number of handshakes is 45.
statements: The unknown value n equals 10.
If the group had 12 people instead, the total number of handshakes would be 66.
The number of ways to choose a committee of 3 people from the n people is 120.
The number of ways to arrange all n people in a single row (n!) is greater than 1,000,000.
If the total number of handshakes had been 55 instead of 45, n would equal 11.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Solve \binom{n}{2} = 45 for n
$$

Solving Cn2 = 45 gives n(n−1) = 90, and n = 10 satisfies this (10·9 = 90), as found in Step 1.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
\binom{12}{2} = 12·11/2 = 66
$$

\binom{12}{2} = 12·11/2 = 66, confirming the statement.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
\binom{10}{3} = 10·9·8/3! = 120
$$

With n = 10, \binom{10}{3} = 10!/(3!·7!) = 120, confirming the statement.

The statement is true.

Statement D — True

$$
10! = 3,628,800
$$

The statement is true.

Statement E — True

$$
Solve \binom{n}{2} = 55 for n
$$

Solving Cn2 = 55 gives n(n−1) = 110, and n = 11 satisfies this (11·10 = 110), confirming the statement.

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Solve for n using the handshake count, where every pair of n people shakes hands exactly once.

tasks.title: Arranging BALLOON
tasks.context: The 7 letters of the word BALLOON (B, A, L, L, O, O, N) are arranged at random in a row. The two L's are identical to each other, and the two O's are identical to each other.
statements: The total number of distinct arrangements is 2,520.
The probability that the two L's are adjacent to each other is 2/7.
The probability that the two L's AND the two O's are both adjacent (each pair sitting together) is greater than 10%.
The probability that the two L's are adjacent equals the probability that the two O's are adjacent.
If all 7 letters had been different (no repeats at all), the total number of arrangements would be less than 2,520.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — False

$$
Total arrangements = 7!/(2!·2!)
$$

The statement is false. Dividing by only one of the two repeated pairs (forgetting either the L's or the O's) gives the tempting but incorrect 2,520 — you must divide by 2! for each repeated letter.

Statement B — True

$$
P(L's adjacent) = (6!/2!)/(7!/(2!·2!)) = 360/1,260 = 2/7
$$

$$
= 360/1,260
$$

= 28.571%.

Gluing the two L's into one block leaves 6 units to arrange, with the two O's still identical among them, giving 6!/2! = 360 arrangements, so P = 2/7, exactly as stated.

The statement is true.

Statement C — False

$$
P(both pairs adjacent) = 5!/(7!/(2!·2!)) = 120/1,260 = 2/21
$$

$$
= 120/1,260
$$

= 9.52%, which is not greater than 10%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement D — True

$$
P(L's adjacent) = P(O's adjacent) = 2/7, by symmetry
$$

$$
= 2/7
$$

= 28.571%.

Both calculations give exactly 360/1,260 by the same symmetric logic — the L's and O's each appear twice, so gluing either pair together leads to an identical count.

The statement is true.

Statement E — False

$$
Compare 7! = 5,040 to 7!/(2!·2!) = 1,260
$$

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true. The disputed claim is "If all 7 letters had been different (no repeats at all), the total number…."
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the multiset permutation formula, since the two L's are identical and the two O's are identical.

tasks.title: A Lottery Draw
tasks.context: A lottery draws 6 numbers, without replacement, from the numbers 1 through 49. A player has chosen 6 numbers in advance and wins a prize based on how many of the drawn numbers match their chosen numbers.
statements: The total number of possible sets of 6 drawn numbers is 13,983,816.
The probability of matching all 6 numbers is less than 1 in 10,000,000.
The probability of matching exactly 3 numbers is greater than 1%.
The probability of matching exactly 3 numbers is greater than the probability of matching exactly 4 numbers.
The probability of matching 0 numbers is greater than 45%.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total combinations = \binom{49}{6}
$$

$$
= 13,983,816
$$

= 13,983,816.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
P(match 6) = 1/\binom{49}{6}
$$

$$
= 1/13,983,816
$$

= 0%.

≈ 0.0000000715, which corresponds to roughly 1 in 14 million — a smaller probability (rarer event) than 1 in 10,000,000, so the statement holds.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
P(match 3) = \binom{6}{3}\cdot \binom{43}{3}/\binom{49}{6}
$$

$$
= 246,820/13,983,816
$$

= 1.765%, which is greater than 1%.

The statement is true.

Statement D — True

$$
Compare \binom{6}{3}\cdot \binom{43}{3} = 246,820 to \binom{6}{4}\cdot \binom{43}{2} = 13,545
$$

= 1.765%.

The statement is true.

Statement E — False

$$
P(match 0) = \binom{43}{6}/\binom{49}{6}
$$

$$
= 6,096,454/13,983,816
$$

= 43.60%, which is not greater than 45%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.
tasks.solution_overview: Use combinations Cnr, permutations P(n,r), and classical probability P(E)=(#favorable)/(#equally likely).

tasks.title: A Round Table
tasks.context: 8 people, including two specific friends A and B, are seated at random around a circular table. Only the relative order of the seats matters - rotating everyone around the table by the same amount counts as the same arrangement, but mirror-image seatings are still counted as different.
statements: The total number of distinct circular arrangements is 5,040.
The probability of event A and B sit next to each other is 2/7.
The probability of event A and B do NOT sit next to each other is less than 70%.
If the same 8 people instead sat in a straight row (not around a table), the probability that A and B are adjacent would be exactly 1/4.
Sitting around a round table makes A and B less likely to end up adjacent than sitting in a straight row would.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total circular arrangements = (n−1)! = 7!
$$

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
P(A, B adjacent) = 2·(n−2)!/(n−1)! = 1,440/5,040 = 2/7
$$

1,440/5,040 simplifies exactly to 2/7, matching the probability from Step 1.

The statement is true.

Statement C — False

$$
P(not adjacent) = 1 − 2/7 = 5/7
$$

$$
= 5/7
$$

= 71.43%, which is not less than 70%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement D — True

$$
P(A, B adjacent, row) = 2·7!/8! = 1/4
$$

$$
= 10,080/40,320
$$

= 25%.

In a row, gluing A and B into a block gives 2·7! = 10,080 arrangements out of 8! = 40,320 total, so P = 1/4 exactly.

The statement is true.

Statement E — False

$$
Compare 2/7
$$

= 28.57%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true (28.57%).
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the circular-arrangement formulas for n = 8 people, comparing to the equivalent row arrangement.

tasks.title: Chevalier de Méré's Dice Problem
tasks.context: A fair six-sided die is rolled 4 times. Separately, a pair of fair six-sided dice is rolled 24 times. (This pair of problems is a famous historical question first posed to Blaise Pascal in the 17th century.)
statements: The probability of rolling at least one 6 in 4 rolls of a single die is greater than 50%.
The probability of rolling at least one 6 in 4 rolls equals 1 − (5/6)⁴.
The probability of rolling no 6 at all in the 4 rolls is less than 45%.
The probability of rolling at least one double-six in 24 rolls of a pair of dice is less than 50%.
The probability of rolling at least one double-six in 24 rolls of a pair of dice is greater than the probability of rolling at least one 6 in 4 rolls of a single die.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
P(at least one 6) = 1 − (5/6)⁴
$$

= 51.77%, which is greater than 50%.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
P(at least one 6 in 4 rolls) = 1 − (5/6)⁴
$$

This is exactly the complement-rule formula applied to 4 independent rolls, each with a 5/6 chance of avoiding a 6.

The statement is true.

Statement C — False

$$
P(no 6 in 4 rolls) = (5/6)⁴
$$

= 48.23%, which is not less than 45%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement D — True

$$
P(at least one double-six) = 1 − (35/36)²⁴
$$

= 49.14%, which is less than 50%.

The statement is true.

Statement E — False

$$
Compare 49.14\% (double-six, 24 rolls) to 51.77\% (single 6, 4 rolls)
$$

= 49.14%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true (49.14%).
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the complement rule to each independent-trials scenario.

tasks.title: A Bookshelf Restriction
tasks.context: 5 distinct fiction novels and 3 distinct mystery novels (8 books total, all different) are arranged at random in a row on a shelf.
statements: The total number of possible arrangements is 40,320.
The number of arrangements in which no two mystery novels are adjacent to each other is 14,400.
The probability that no two mystery novels are adjacent is 5/14.
The probability that all three mystery novels are adjacent (sitting together as a block) is greater than the probability that no two mystery novels are adjacent.
The probability that no two mystery novels are adjacent is more than 3 times the probability that all three mystery novels are adjacent.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total arrangements = 8!
$$

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
No-two-adjacent arrangements = 5!·{}_{6}P_{3} = 120·120 = 14,400
$$

Arranging the 5 fiction novels (5! ways) and placing the 3 mystery novels into 3 of the 6 available gaps in order (_6P_3 = 120 ways) gives 5!·_6P_3 = 120·120 = 14,400.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
P(no two mystery novels adjacent) = 14,400/40,320 = 5/14
$$

14,400/40,320 simplifies exactly to 5/14, matching the probability from Step 1.

The statement is true.

Statement D — False

$$
Compare 3/28
$$

$$
= 3/28
$$

= 35.71%.

P(no two adjacent) = 5/14

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement E — True

$$
Compare (5/14)/(3/28) = 10/3
$$

$$
= 140/42
$$

= 3.33.

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the gap method: arrange the 5 fiction novels first, then place the 3 mystery novels into the gaps between and around them.

tasks.title: Find the Missing Value (12)
tasks.context: A security code is formed by arranging 3 different digits, in order, chosen from a set of n available digits (no digit repeats within a code). The total number of possible 3-digit codes is 336.
statements: The unknown value n equals 8.
If codes were instead 4 digits long (still no repeats, still order matters, same n), the number of possible codes would be 1,680.
The number of ways to choose (unordered) 3 digits from the n available digits is 56.
If the number of possible 3-digit codes had been 720 instead of 336, n would equal 10.
The number of ways to arrange all n digits in a row (n!) is greater than 50,000.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Solve {}_{n}P_{3} = 336 for n
$$

Solving _nP_3 = 336 gives n(n−1)(n−2) = 336, and n = 8 satisfies this (8·7·6 = 336), as found in Step 1.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
{}_{8}P_{4} = 8·7·6·5 = 1,680
$$

With n = 8, _8P_4 = 8·7·6·5 = 1,680, confirming the statement.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
\binom{8}{3} = 8·7·6/3! = 56
$$

With n = 8, C83 = 8!/(3!·5!) = 56, confirming the statement.

The statement is true.

Statement D — True

$$
Solve n(n−1)(n−2) = 720 for n
$$

Re-solving n(n−1)(n−2) = 720 gives n = 10, since 10·9·8 = 720, confirming the statement.

The statement is true.

Statement E — False

$$
8! = 40,320
$$

The statement is false. 8! = 40,320, — it is somewhat less worth double-checking rather than assuming factorials are always "large."
tasks.solution_overview: Solve for n using the permutation count, since the 3-digit code has order-matters and no-repeats.

tasks.title: A Poker Hand (13)
tasks.context: A 5-card hand is dealt at random, without replacement, from a standard 52-card deck (13 ranks × 4 suits, no jokers).
statements: The total number of distinct 5-card hands that can be dealt is 2,598,960.
The probability of getting exactly one pair (one rank appears twice, and the other three cards are all different ranks) is greater than 42.3%.
The probability of a full house (three cards of one rank, two of another) is exactly 6 times the probability of four of a kind.
The probability of getting two pair is greater than the probability of getting exactly one pair.
The probability of a full house is greater than 1 in 700.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total hands = \binom{52}{5}
$$

$$
= 2,598,960
$$

= 2,598,960.

The statement is true.

Statement B — False

$$
P(one pair) = [\binom{13}{1}\cdot \binom{4}{2}·\binom{12}{3}·4³]/\binom{52}{5}
$$

= 42.2569%, which is not greater than 42.3%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement C — True

$$
P(full house)/P(four of a kind) = 3,744/624 = 6
$$

Both probabilities share the same denominator \binom{52}{5}, so their ratio equals the ratio of the raw counts: 3,744 / 624 = 6 exactly.

The statement is true.

Statement D — False

$$
Compare 123,552 to 1,098,240 (same denominator \binom{52}{5})
$$

= 4.7539%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true (4.754%).

Statement E — True

$$
P(full house)
$$

$$
= 3,744/2,598,960
$$

= 100%.

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the multiplication principle to count each hand type: choose which rank(s) fill each structural role, then choose suits for the cards occupying that role.

tasks.title: Choosing a Committee
tasks.context: A club has 8 men and 5 women (13 members total). A committee of 5 members is selected at random from the 13.
statements: The total number of possible 5-person committees is 1,287.
The probability that the committee has exactly 3 men and 2 women is greater than 43.5%.
The probability that the committee has at least 4 women is less than 3.2%.
It is impossible for the committee to contain no men at all, since only 5 women are available.
The probability that the committee includes at least 1 woman is more than 30 times the probability that it includes at least 4 women.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total committees = \binom{13}{5}
$$

$$
= 1,287
$$

= 1,287.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
P(3M, 2W) = \binom{8}{3}\cdot \binom{5}{2}/\binom{13}{5} = 560/1,287
$$

$$
= 560/1,287
$$

= 43.5120%.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
P(≥4 women) = [\binom{8}{1}\cdot \binom{5}{4} + \binom{5}{5}]/\binom{13}{5} = 41/1,287
$$

$$
= 41/1,287
$$

= 3.1857%.

The statement is true.

Statement D — False

$$
Ways with 0 men = \binom{8}{0}\cdot \binom{5}{5} = 1
$$

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement E — True

$$
[\binom{13}{5} − \binom{8}{5}]/[\binom{8}{1}\cdot \binom{5}{4} + \binom{5}{5}] = 1,231/41
$$

= 30.0244.

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the combination formula Cnr to the men and women pools separately, then combine the two counts via the multiplication principle for each case.

tasks.title: Mismatched Gifts (Derangements)
tasks.context: 6 friends each bring one wrapped gift to a party. The gifts are shuffled and redistributed uniformly at random, one to each friend - every one of the 6! possible assignments is equally likely.
statements: The total number of ways to redistribute the 6 gifts is 720.
The probability that no friend receives their own gift is greater than 36.8%.
The probability that exactly one friend receives their own gift is greater than the probability that no friend receives their own gift.
The probability that exactly two friends receive their own gifts is exactly 3/16.
The probability that every friend receives their own original gift (the identity assignment) is greater than 1 in 500.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
Total assignments = 6!
$$

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
P(no matches) = D₆/6! = 265/720
$$

$$
= 265/720
$$

= 36.8056%.

The statement is true.

Statement C — False

$$
Compare \binom{6}{1}·D₅/6! = 264/720 to D₆/6! = 265/720
$$

$$
= 264/720
$$

= 36.6667%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement D — True

$$

tasks.title: A Birthday Coincidence
tasks.context: 8 unrelated people are in a room. Assume 365 equally likely birthdays (ignore leap years) and that each person's birthday is independent of everyone else's.
statements: The probability that no two of the 8 people share a birthday is greater than 92.5%.
The probability that at least two of the 8 people share a birthday is greater than 7.4%.
The probability that at least one of the other 7 people has the exact same birthday as one specific named person (say, the first person to enter the room) is less than 2%.
The probability that at least two people (any two, not a specific pair) share a birthday is more than 3.9 times the probability that someone shares that one specific person's birthday.
If the group size were increased to 23 people, the probability that at least two share a birthday would exceed 50%.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — True

$$
P(no match) = (365·364·⋯·358)/365⁸
$$

= 92.5665%.

The statement is true.

Statement B — True

$$
P(≥2 share) = 1 − (365·364·⋯·358)/365⁸
$$

$$
= 1 - 0.925665
$$

= 7.4335%.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$
P(match a specific person) = 1 − (364/365)⁷
$$

= 1.9021%, which is less than 2%.

The statement is true.

Statement D — True

$$
0.074335/0.019021
$$

= 3.9080.

The statement is true.

Statement E — True

$$
P(≥2 share, n=23) = 1 − (365·364·⋯·343)/365²³
$$

= 50.7297%.

This is the famous classical result: at n = 23, P(at least two share a birthday) ≈ 50.7297%, which exceeds 50% — a far smaller group than most people's intuition would suggest. ≈ 0.507297

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the complement rule: P(no shared birthday among n people) = [365·364·⋯·(365−n+1)] / 365ⁿ.

tasks.title: Distributing Candies (Stars and Bars)

statements: The total number of distinct ways to distribute the 10 candies among the 4 children is 286.

The probability that a specific child receives at least 5 candies is less than 20%.

$$
Total distributions = \binom{10 + 4 − 1}{4 − 1} = \binom{13}{3}
$$

$$
= 286
$$

= 286.

Statement B — True

P(specific child gets 0) = \binom{12}{2}/\binom{13}{3} = 66/286
$$

$$
= 66/286
$$

= 23.0769%.

The statement is true.

Statement C — True

$$

$$
= 56/286
$$

= 19.5804%.

The statement is true.

Statement D — True

$$
P(all ≥ 1) = \binom{9}{3}/\binom{13}{3} = 84/286 = 42/143
$$

$$
= 84/286,

which simplifies exactly to 42/143 ≈ 29.3706%.

$$
Compare 66/286
$$

= 1.1786.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the stars-and-bars formula: the number of ways to distribute n identical items among k distinct groups is Cn + k − 1k − 1.

tasks.title: Repeated Digits in a PIN
tasks.context: A 4-digit PIN code is generated at random by independently choosing each of the 4 digits from 0-9. Digits may repeat, and every one of the 10,000 possible codes is equally likely.
statements: The total number of possible 4-digit PIN codes, allowing repeated digits, is 5,040.
The probability that all four digits are different (no repeats at all) is greater than 55%.
The probability that at least one digit repeats somewhere in the code is greater than 49%.
The probability of exactly one repeated pair (two digits the same, and the other two digits distinct from each other and from the pair) is greater than 45%.
The probability that all four digits are identical is greater than 1 in 500.
tactical_explanations:
Statement A — False

$$
Total codes (repeats allowed) = 10⁴ = 10,000
$$

The statement is false. The true total, allowing repeats, is 10⁴ = 10,000 — a classic mix-up between the overall total and one restricted case within it.

Statement B — False

$$
P(all different) = {}_{10}P_{4}/10⁴ = 5,040/10,000 = 0.504
$$

$$
= 5,040/10,000 = 50.4%
$$

= 50.4%, which is not greater than 55%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true.

Statement C — True

$$
P(at least one repeat) = 1 − {}_{10}P_{4}/10⁴ = 1 − 0.504 = 0.496
$$

$$
= 1 - 0.504
$$

= 49.6%, which is greater than 49%.

The statement is true.

Statement D — False

$$
P(exactly one pair) = 10·\binom{4}{2}·9·8/10⁴ = 4,320/10,000 = 0.432
$$

$$
= 4,320/10,000 = 43.2%
$$

= 43.2%, which is not greater than 45%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true (43.2%).

Statement E — False

$$
P(all identical) = 10/10⁴ = 1/1,000 vs. 1/500 = 0.2\%
$$

$$
= 10/10,000 = 0.1%
$$

= 0.1%.

The statement is false. A student who applied the complementary count or swapped the inequality direction would mark the statement true (10%).
tasks.solution_overview: Count total codes by the multiplication principle (10 choices for each of the 4 digits, repetition allowed), then use complementary counting and case-by-case counting for the repeat patterns.

tasks.title: The Assessment Poster
tasks.context: For a campus assessment fair, ten letter tiles spelling the word ASSESSMENT (A, S, S, E, S, S, M, E, N, T) are placed in a bag and drawn out one at a time to form a poster headline in a row. = 3.333%.

Statement E — True

$$
P(M,T adjacent) = 2·[9!/(4!·2!)]/[10!/(4!·2!)] = 1/5 = P(E's adjacent)
$$

$$
= 1/5
$$

= 20%.

The statement is true.
tasks.solution_overview: Apply the multiset permutation formula (repeats: S×4, E×2), then use the block method for each adjacency event.

tasks.title: Tennis Club Pairings

= 100%

Chebyshev's inequality guarantees that the probability that X is less than 30 or greater than 70 is at most 0.0625.

Because the Chebyshev bound for the probability of given X - 50 given is at least 12.5 works out to exactly 0.16, the true value of the probability of given X - 50 given is at least 12.5 must also equal 0.16.
Using k = 3 instead of k = 2 in the inequality the probability of given X - μ given is at least kσ is at most 1/k² produces a tighter (smaller) upper bound on the tail probability.

$$

= 1 - 0.25

= 75%.

$$

= 1 - 1

= 1/16

$$

= 0.111.

tasks.title: Late Computer Deliveries
tasks.context: Company A supplies 40% of the computers sold and is late 5% of the time. Company B supplies 30% of the computers sold and is late 3% of the time. Company C supplies the remaining 30% and is late 2.5% of the time. A computer arrives late.
statements: P(a randomly selected computer arrives late) is greater than 3.5%.
P(the computer came from Company A, given that it arrived late) is greater than 54%.
P(the computer came from Company B, given that it arrived late) is greater than 25%.
P(the computer came from Company C, given that it arrived late) is less than 20%.
P(the computer came from Company A, given that it arrived late) is more than 2.6 times P(the computer came from Company C, given that it arrived late).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The event can happen through any one of the sources, so the law of total probability adds each source's share of it:

$$
P(\text{Late}) = \sum P(\text{Source}) \times P(\text{Late} \mid \text{Source})
$$

$$
P(\text{late}) = P(A) \times P(\text{late} \mid A) + P(B) \times P(\text{late} \mid B) + P(C) \times P(\text{late} \mid C) = 0.40 \times 0.05 + 0.30 \times 0.03 + 0.30 \times 0.025 = 0.020+0.009+0.0075 = 0.0365 = 3.65\%
$$

This is is above 3.5%.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(A \mid \text{Late}) =\frac{(P(A) \times P(\text{Late} \mid A))}{P(\text{Late})}
$$

$$
P(A \mid \text{late}) =\frac{P(A) \times P(\text{late} \mid A)}{P(\text{late})}=\frac{0.020}{0.0365}\approx 54.795\%
$$

This is is above 54%.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(B \mid \text{Late}) =\frac{(P(B) \times P(\text{Late} \mid B))}{P(\text{Late})}
$$

$P(B \mid \text{late}) =\frac{P(B) \times P(\text{late} \mid B)}{P(\text{late})}=\frac{0.009}{0.0365}\approx 24.658\%$, which is below 25%, not above it.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → False

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(C \mid \text{Late}) =\frac{(P(C) \times P(\text{Late} \mid C))}{P(\text{Late})}
$$

$P(C \mid \text{late}) =\frac{P(C) \times P(\text{late} \mid C)}{P(\text{late})}=\frac{0.0075}{0.0365}\approx 20.548\%$, which is above 20%, not below it.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Both posteriors are divided by the same total, so their ratio is simply the ratio of the two numerators:

$$
\frac{(P(A) \times P(\text{Late} \mid A))}{(P(C) \times P(\text{Late} \mid C))}
$$

$P(A \mid \text{late}) \approx 54.795\%$ and $P(C \mid \text{late}) \approx 20.548\%$ (from statements B and D).

Since both share the denominator $P(\text{late})$, the ratio is just $P(A) \times P(\text{late} \mid A)$ divided by $P(C) \times P(\text{late} \mid C) =\frac{0.020}{0.0075}\approx 2.667$ which is above 2.6.

So the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Every source in this scenario can produce the observed event, so the work happens in two moves. First the law of total probability collects the whole event probability by weighting each source's own rate by how often that source is used:

$$
P(E) = \sum_i P(S_i)\,P(E \mid S_i)
$$

Then Bayes' theorem reverses the direction of the conditioning. Once the event is known to have happened, a source's posterior share is its own contribution to the event divided by the total:

$$
P(S_i \mid E) = \frac{P(S_i)\,P(E \mid S_i)}{P(E)}
$$

A source with a small share can still end up with a large posterior when its own event rate is high, so every statement below has to be checked against the arithmetic rather than against intuition.

tasks.title: Contaminated Drug Batches
tasks.context: A pharmaceutical company sources a drug from three manufacturing plants. Plant X produces 50% of all batches and has a 1.2% contamination rate. Plant Y produces 35% of all batches and has a 0.8% contamination rate. Plant Z produces the remaining 15% and has a 2.0% contamination rate. A batch tests positive for contamination.
statements: P(a randomly selected batch is contaminated) is greater than 1.15%.
P(the batch came from Plant X, given that it is contaminated) is greater than 51%.
P(the batch came from Plant Z, given that it is contaminated) is greater than P(the batch came from Plant Y, given that it is contaminated).
P(the batch came from Plant Y, given that it is contaminated) is greater than 24%.
P(the batch came from Plant Z, given that it is contaminated) is less than 26%.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{Contaminated}) = \sum P(\text{Plant}) \times P(\text{Contaminated} \mid \text{Plant})
$$

$$
P(\text{contaminated}) = 0.50 \times 0.012 + 0.35 \times 0.008 + 0.15 \times 0.020 = 0.0060+0.0028+0.0030 = 0.0118 = 1.18\%
$$

This is is above 1.15%.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → False

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(X \mid \text{Contaminated}) =\frac{(P(X) \times P(\text{Contaminated} \mid X))}{P(\text{Contaminated})}
$$

$P(X \mid \text{contaminated}) =\frac{0.0060}{0.0118}\approx 50.847\%$, which is below 51%, not above it.

So the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The claim is a comparison, so we work out both sides and line them up.

$$
P(Z \mid \text{Contaminated}) =\frac{(P(Z) \times P(\text{Contaminated} \mid Z))}{P(\text{Contaminated})}
$$

$$
P(Y \mid \text{Contaminated}) =\frac{(P(Y) \times P(\text{Contaminated} \mid Y))}{P(\text{Contaminated})}
$$

$$
P(Z \mid \text{contaminated}) =\frac{0.0030}{0.0118}\approx 25.424\%, \text{and} P(Y \mid \text{contaminated}) =\frac{0.0028}{0.0118}\approx 23.729\%
$$

Since 25.424% is greater than 23.729%, the statement holds, note this reverses the plants' prior order (Y's prior of 35% is larger than Z's prior of 15%), because Z's much higher contamination rate outweighs its smaller market share.

So the statement is True.

**D.** → False

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(Y \mid \text{Contaminated}) =\frac{(P(Y) \times P(\text{Contaminated} \mid Y))}{P(\text{Contaminated})}
$$

$P(Y \mid \text{contaminated}) \approx 23.729\%$ (from statement C), which is below 24%, not above it.

So the statement is False.

**E.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(Z \mid \text{Contaminated}) =\frac{(P(Z) \times P(\text{Contaminated} \mid Z))}{P(\text{Contaminated})}
$$

$P(Z \mid \text{contaminated}) \approx 25.424\%$ (from statement C), which is below 26%.

So the statement is True.

$$

$$

$$

Every source in this scenario can produce the observed event, so the work happens in two moves. First the law of total probability collects the whole event probability by weighting each source's own rate by how often that source is used:

$$

$$

Then Bayes' theorem reverses the direction of the conditioning. Once the event is known to have happened, a source's posterior share is its own contribution to the event divided by the total:

tasks.title: Trail Closures and the Weather
tasks.context: A mountain hiking trail is affected by daily weather. Of all days, 55% are Sunny, 30% are Rainy, and 15% are Snowy. The trail is closed for safety on 2% of Sunny days, 10% of Rainy days, and 40% of Snowy days. Today, the trail is closed.
statements: P(the trail is closed on a random day) is greater than 8%.
P(the day is Snowy AND the trail is closed) equals 6%.
P(the day is Snowy, given the trail is closed) is greater than 65%.
P(the trail is open) equals 1 minus P(the trail is closed).
P(the day is Rainy, given the trail is closed) is greater than P(the day is Sunny, given the trail is closed).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{Closed}) = \sum P(\text{weather}) \times P(\text{Closed} \mid \text{weather})
$$

We just calculated $P(\text{Closed}) = 10.1\%$, which is indeed greater than 8%.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(W \cap \text{Closed}) = P(W) \times P(\text{Closed} \mid W)
$$

The joint probability of two events happening together is found by simple multiplication, no division needed yet, since we are not conditioning on anything.

$$
P(\text{Snowy AND Closed}) = P(W) \times P(\text{Closed} \mid W) = 0.15 \times 0.40 = 0.06
$$

This is is exactly 6%.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(W \mid \text{Closed}) =\frac{P(W \cap \text{Closed})}{P(\text{Closed})}
$$

Now we want a posterior probability: given that we already know the trail is closed, how likely is it that today is Snowy? This is where Bayes' Theorem comes in, divide Snowy's own joint probability by the total $P(\text{Closed})$ we found above.

$$
P(\text{Snowy} \mid \text{Closed}) =\frac{P(W \cap \text{Closed})}{P(\text{Closed})}=\frac{0.06}{0.101}\approx 0.594 = 59.4\%
$$

59.4% is not greater than 65%, so this statement is false, even though Snowy days close the trail most often, they're rare enough (only 15% of days) that they don't account for as much as two-thirds of all closures.

**D.** → True

The rule the claim needs is:

$$
P(\text{Open}) = 1 - P(\text{Closed})
$$

'Open' and 'Closed' cover every possibility for the trail on a given day, there is no third option, so they are complementary events, meaning their probabilities must add to 100%.

This makes $P(\text{Open}) = 1 - P(\text{Closed})$ true by definition, regardless of what the actual numbers are.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The claim is a comparison, so we work out both sides and line them up.

$$
\frac{P(R \cap \text{Closed})}{P(\text{Closed})}
$$

$$
\frac{P(S \cap \text{Closed})}{P(\text{Closed})}
$$

To compare, we need both posterior probabilities.

We already have the total $P(\text{Closed}) = 0.101$ so we just need each weather type's joint probability from Step 2's calculation.

$$
P(\text{Rainy} \mid \text{Closed}) =\frac{(0.30 \times 0.10)}{0.101}=\frac{0.030}{0.101}\approx 29.7\%
$$

$$
P(\text{Sunny} \mid \text{Closed}) =\frac{(0.55 \times 0.02)}{0.101}=\frac{0.011}{0.101}\approx 10.9\%
$$

Since 29.7% is greater than 10.9%, the statement is true, Rainy days are a much more common explanation for a closure than Sunny days, even though Sunny days happen far more often overall, because Rainy days close the trail five times as often.

tasks.title: Fungus Across Three Tree Species
tasks.context: A forest is made up of three tree species: Oak (50% of all trees), Pine (35%), and Birch (15%). A certain fungus infects 2% of Oaks, 5% of Pines, and 12% of Birches. A randomly examined tree is found to be infected with the fungus.

P(the tree is a Birch, given it is infected) is greater than 45%.

$$

$$

We just found $P(\text{Infected}) = 4.55\%$, which is greater than 4%.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(B \cap \text{Infected}) = P(B) \times P(\text{Infected} \mid B)
$$

This is a joint probability, so we simply multiply Birch's share of the forest by its infection rate, no division is needed since we're not conditioning on anything yet.

$$
P(\text{Birch AND Infected}) = P(B) \times P(\text{Infected} \mid B) = 0.15 \times 0.12 = 0.018, \text{exactly} 1.8\%
$$

So the statement is True.

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(B \mid \text{Infected}) =\frac{P(B \cap \text{Infected})}{P(\text{Infected})}
$$

Now we condition the other direction: given that an examined tree is infected, what's the chance it's a Birch? Divide Birch's joint probability by the overall $P(\text{Infected})$ we calculated above.

$$
P(\text{Birch} \mid \text{Infected}) =\frac{0.018}{0.0455}\approx 0.396 = 39.6\%
$$

39.6% is not greater than 45%, so the statement is false.

Birch trees have the highest infection rate of the three species, but they make up only 15% of the forest, which caps how much they can contribute to the total infected population.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The rule the claim needs is:

$$
P(\text{not Infected}) = 1 - P(\text{Infected})
$$

A tree is either infected or it isn't, there's no third possibility, so these two events are complementary and their probabilities must sum to 100%.

So the statement is True.

$$
\frac{P(P \cap \text{Infected})}{P(\text{Infected})}
$$

$$
\frac{P(O \cap \text{Infected})}{P(\text{Infected})}
$$

We compare two posterior probabilities, both using the same denominator, $P(\text{Infected}) = 0.0455$

$$
P(\text{Pine} \mid \text{Infected}) =\frac{(0.35 \times 0.05)}{0.0455}=\frac{0.0175}{0.0455}\approx 38.5\%
$$

$$
P(\text{Oak} \mid \text{Infected}) =\frac{(0.50 \times 0.02)}{0.0455}=\frac{0.010}{0.0455}\approx 22.0\%
$$

Since 38.5% is greater than 22.0%, the statement is true, even though Oak is the most common tree in the forest, Pine's higher infection rate (5% vs.

2%) more than makes up for its smaller share, so a randomly infected tree is more likely to be a Pine than an Oak.

So the statement is True.

$$

$$

$$

34.8% is not greater than 40%, so the statement is False, even though Catfish has the single highest individual tagging rate (8%) of the three species.

tasks.title: A Commuter Running Late
tasks.context: On a given workday, a commuter walks to work 20% of the time, bikes 30% of the time, and drives 50% of the time. They arrive late 15% of the time when walking, 8% of the time when biking, and 5% of the time when driving. Today, the commuter arrives late.
statements: P(the commuter arrives late) is greater than 7%.
P(the commuter walked AND arrived late) equals 3%.
P(the commuter walked, given they arrived late) is greater than 40%.
P(the commuter arrives on time) equals 1 minus P(the commuter arrives late).
P(the commuter biked, given they arrived late) is less than P(the commuter drove, given they arrived late).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{Late}) = \sum P(\text{mode}) \times P(\text{Late} \mid \text{mode})
$$

We just found $P(\text{Late}) = 7.9\%$, which is greater than 7%.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{Wa} \cap \text{Late}) = P(\text{Wa}) \times P(\text{Late} \mid \text{Wa})
$$

Multiply the probability of walking by the probability of being late given walking.

$$
P(\text{Walked AND Late}) = P(\text{Wa}) \times P(\text{Late} \mid \text{Wa}) = 0.20 \times 0.15 = 0.030, \text{exactly} 3\%
$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{Wa} \mid \text{Late}) =\frac{P(\text{Wa} \cap \text{Late})}{P(\text{Late})}
$$

Divide Walking's joint probability (from part B) by the overall $P(\text{Late})$.

$$
P(\text{Walked} \mid \text{Late}) =\frac{0.030}{0.079}\approx 0.380 = 38.0\%
$$

38.0% is not greater than 40%, so the statement is False, walking has the highest individual late rate (15%), but the commuter only walks 20% of the time, which limits how much walking can contribute to total lateness.

**D.** → True

The rule the claim needs is:

$$
P(\text{on time}) = 1 - P(\text{Late})
$$

Arriving late and arriving on time are the only two possibilities, so they are complementary events and their probabilities sum to 100%.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

$$
\frac{P(\text{Bi} \cap \text{Late})}{P(\text{Late})}
$$

$$
\frac{P(\text{Dr} \cap \text{Late})}{P(\text{Late})}
$$

Find both remaining joint probabilities, then divide each by $P(\text{Late}) = 0.079$

$$
P(\text{Biked} \mid \text{Late}) =\frac{(0.30 \times 0.08)}{0.079}=\frac{0.024}{0.079}\approx 30.4\%
$$

$$
P(\text{Drove} \mid \text{Late}) =\frac{(0.50 \times 0.05)}{0.079}=\frac{0.025}{0.079}\approx 31.6\%
$$

Since 30.4% is less than 31.6%, the statement is true, though only by a narrow margin, this is a case where you need to carry out the full division rather than guessing, since biking has a lower late rate but driving is used much more often.

tasks.title: Meteors Spotted Under Cloud Cover
tasks.context: During a meteor shower, the sky is Clear on 40% of nights, Partly Cloudy on 35% of nights, and Overcast on 25% of nights. An observer spots at least one meteor on 25% of Clear nights, 10% of Partly Cloudy nights, and 2% of Overcast nights. Tonight, the observer spots a meteor.
statements: P(a meteor is spotted on a random night) is greater than 12%.
P(the sky is Clear AND a meteor is spotted) equals 10%.
P(the sky is Clear, given a meteor is spotted) is greater than 75%.
P(no meteor is spotted) equals 1 minus P(a meteor is spotted).
P(the sky is Partly Cloudy, given a meteor is spotted) is greater than P(the sky is Overcast, given a meteor is spotted).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{Spotted}) = \sum P(\text{sky}) \times P(\text{Spotted} \mid \text{sky})
$$

We just found $P(\text{Spotted}) = 14\%$, which is greater than 12%.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(C \cap \text{Spotted}) = P(C) \times P(\text{Spotted} \mid C)
$$

Multiply the probability of a Clear night by the probability of spotting a meteor given a Clear night.

$$
P(\text{Clear AND Spotted}) = P(C) \times P(\text{Spotted} \mid C) = 0.40 \times 0.25 = 0.100, \text{exactly} 10\%
$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(C \mid \text{Spotted}) =\frac{P(C \cap \text{Spotted})}{P(\text{Spotted})}
$$

Divide Clear's joint probability (from part B) by the overall $P(\text{Spotted})$.

$$
P(\text{Clear} \mid \text{Spotted}) =\frac{0.100}{0.140}\approx 0.714 = 71.4\%
$$

71.4% is not greater than 75%, so the statement is False, Clear nights dominate the spotted-meteor cases, since they're both the most common sky condition and have by far the best spotting rate, but they still fall just short of three-quarters of all sightings.

**D.** → True

The rule the claim needs is:

$$
P(\text{no meteor spotted}) = 1 - P(\text{Spotted})
$$

Spotting a meteor and not spotting one are the only two outcomes for the night, so they are complementary and their probabilities sum to 100%.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The claim is a comparison, so we work out both sides and line them up.

$$
\frac{P(\text{Pc} \cap \text{Spotted})}{P(\text{Spotted})}
$$

$$
\frac{P(\text{Ov} \cap \text{Spotted})}{P(\text{Spotted})}
$$

Find both remaining joint probabilities, then divide each by $P(\text{Spotted}) = 0.140$

$$
P(\text{Partly Cloudy} \mid \text{Spotted}) =\frac{(0.35 \times 0.10)}{0.140}=\frac{0.035}{0.140}= 25.0\%
$$

$$
P(\text{Overcast} \mid \text{Spotted}) =\frac{(0.25 \times 0.02)}{0.140}=\frac{0.005}{0.140}\approx 3.6\%
$$

Since 25.0% is greater than 3.6%, the statement is true, Overcast nights are both less common and much worse for spotting meteors, so they contribute only a small fraction of all sightings.

**Note.** In every question, the same two-step process applies no matter how different the story sounds, first add up every category's (prior times likelihood) to get the total probability of the evidence, then divide any one category's own (prior times likelihood) by that total to get its posterior probability. Question 78 (statement C) shows this can produce ties: if two categories happen to have the same joint probability, they will have the same posterior probability, even with very different prior probabilities and likelihoods individually.

So the statement is True.

tasks.title: Two Days Without a Crane Sighting
tasks.context: A birder visits one of three habitats to look for a rare crane: Wetland (40% of visits), Grassland (35%), or Forest (25%). On any given day, the probability of spotting the crane is 20% in the Wetland, 8% in the Grassland, and 3% in the Forest, independently from day to day. The birder visits the same habitat on two consecutive days and does NOT spot the crane on either day.
statements: P(no crane is spotted on either of the two days, overall) is greater than 75%.
P(the habitat is Wetland AND no crane is spotted on either day) equals 25.6%.
P(the habitat is Wetland, given no crane was spotted on either day) is greater than 35%.
P(the crane is spotted on at least one of the two days) equals 1 minus P(no crane is spotted on either day).
P(the habitat is Grassland, given no crane was spotted on either day) is greater than P(the habitat is Forest, given no crane was spotted on either day).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{miss both}) = \sum P(\text{habitat}) \times (1-P(\text{spot} \mid \text{habitat}))^{2}
$$

We just found $P(\text{miss both days}) \approx 78.75\%$, which is greater than 75%.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{We} \cap \text{miss both}) = P(\text{We}) \times (1-P(\text{spot} \mid \text{We}))^{2}
$$

Multiply Wetland's prior by its two-day miss probability, found above.

$$
P(\text{Wetland} \cap \text{miss both}) = 0.40 \times 0.64 = 0.256, \text{exactly} 25.6\%
$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{We} \mid \text{miss both}) =\frac{P(\text{We} \cap \text{miss both})}{P(\text{miss both})}
$$

Divide Wetland's joint probability by the total $P(\text{miss both}) = 0.787465$

$$
P(\text{Wetland} \mid \text{miss both}) =\frac{0.256}{0.787465}\approx 0.3251 = 32.5\%
$$

32.5% is not greater than 35%, so the statement is false.

Even though the Wetland has by far the highest single-day spot rate (making two straight misses there feel surprising), it's also the largest prior category, and two independent misses only push its posterior down moderately.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The rule the claim needs is:

$$
P(\text{spot} \ge 1 \text{day}) = 1 - P(\text{miss both days})
$$

'Spotted on at least one day' and 'missed on both days' are complementary events, there is no overlap and no gap between them.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The claim is a comparison, so we work out both sides and line them up.

$$
\frac{P(\text{Gr} \cap \text{miss both})}{P(\text{miss both})}
$$

$$
\frac{P(\text{Fo} \cap \text{miss both})}{P(\text{miss both})}
$$

Divide each remaining joint probability by $P(\text{miss both}) = 0.787465$

$$
P(\text{Grassland} \mid \text{miss both}) =\frac{(0.35 \times 0.8464)}{0.787465}=\frac{0.29624}{0.787465}\approx 37.6\%
$$

$$
P(\text{Forest} \mid \text{miss both}) =\frac{(0.25 \times 0.9409)}{0.787465}=\frac{0.235225}{0.787465}\approx 29.9\%
$$

Since 37.6% is greater than 29.9%, the statement is true, Grassland ends up the single most likely habitat after two misses, even though the Wetland started out with the highest individual spot rate, because two consecutive misses are much more surprising (and thus much stronger evidence against) a habitat where cranes are usually easy to see.

tasks.title: Coral Bleaching Across Four Reefs
tasks.context: A marine biologist surveys coral across four reef zones: North (35% of all coral), South (30%), East (20%), and West (15%). The observed coral-bleaching rate is 10% in the North, 15% in the South, 25% in the East, and 40% in the West. A randomly sampled piece of coral shows signs of bleaching.
statements: P(a coral sample shows bleaching) is greater than 15%.
P(the coral is from the West Reef AND shows bleaching) equals 6%.
P(the coral is from the West Reef, given it shows bleaching) is greater than 35%.
P(the coral shows no bleaching) equals 1 minus P(the coral shows bleaching).
P(the coral is from the East Reef, given it shows bleaching AND is known not to be from the West Reef) is greater than 35%.

**A.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{bleach}) = \sum P(\text{reef}) \times P(\text{bleach} \mid \text{reef})
$$

We just found $P(\text{bleach}) = 19\%$, which is greater than 15%.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(W \cap \text{bleach}) = P(W) \times P(\text{bleach} \mid W)
$$

Multiply West's prior by its bleaching rate.

$$
P(\text{West} \cap \text{bleach}) = 0.15 \times 0.40 = 0.06, \text{exactly} 6\%
$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(W \mid \text{bleach}) =\frac{P(W \cap \text{bleach})}{P(\text{bleach})}
$$

Divide West's joint probability by the total $P(\text{bleach}) = 0.19$

$$
P(\text{West} \mid \text{bleach}) =\frac{0.06}{0.19}\approx 0.3158 = 31.6\%
$$

31.6% is not greater than 35%, so the statement is False, West has the highest bleaching rate by far, but it's also the smallest reef zone, which caps its share of all bleached samples.

**D.** → True

The rule the claim needs is:

$$
P(\text{no bleach}) = 1 - P(\text{bleach})
$$

'Bleaching' and 'no bleaching' are the only two outcomes for a sample, so they are complementary.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(E \mid \text{bleach}, \text{not W}) =\frac{P(E \cap \text{bleach})}{(P(N \cap \text{bleach}) + P(S \cap \text{bleach}) + P(E \cap \text{bleach}))}
$$

This statement adds a condition: we now know the coral is NOT from the West Reef, in addition to knowing it's bleached.

This shrinks our sample space to only North, South, and East, so we must renormalize by dividing by the sum of just those three joint probabilities, not by the full $P(\text{bleach})$.

The three relevant joint probabilities (from the Step 2 calculation) are:

$$
\text{North} = 0.035, \text{South} = 0.045, \text{East} = 0.05
$$

$$
\text{These sum to} 0.035+0.045+0.05 = 0.13
$$

$P(\text{East} \mid \text{bleach AND not West}) =\frac{P(\text{East} \cap \text{bleach})}{(\text{sum of North}, \text{South}, \text{East joint probabilities})}=\frac{0.05}{0.13}\approx 0.3846 = 38.5\%$, which is greater than 35%.

Notice this is larger than the plain $P(\text{East} \mid \text{bleach}) \approx 26.3\%$ from a standard Bayes calculation, ruling out West Reef entirely reassigns its share of the probability to the remaining three zones, boosting each of their posteriors.

So the statement is True.

tasks.title: A Failed Night at the Observatory
tasks.context: An observatory classifies nights into five cloud-cover bands: Band 1, 0–20% cover (15% of nights); Band 2, 20–40% (25%); Band 3, 40–60% (30%); Band 4, 60–80% (20%); Band 5, 80–100% (10%). Band 1:

$$
1-0.90 = 0.10
$$

Band 2:

$$
1-0.70 = 0.30
$$

Band 3:

$$
1-0.40 = 0.60
$$

Band 4:

$$
1-0.15 = 0.85
$$

Band 5:

$$
1-0.03 = 0.97
$$

$$

$$

53.7%.

tasks.title: Two Clues and Three Suspects
tasks.context: A wildlife tracker suspects one of three animals is active in an area: Coyote (50% prior probability), Fox (30%), or Bobcat (20%). Given the species, the probability of leaving a large paw print is 70% for Coyote, 20% for Fox, and 55% for Bobcat; independently, the probability that any scat found contains fur is 60% for Coyote, 80% for Fox, and 40% for Bobcat. At the site, the tracker finds BOTH a large paw print AND fur-containing scat (assume these two clues are independent of each other once you know the species).
statements: P(both clues are found, overall) is greater than 25%.
P(the species is Coyote AND both clues are found) equals 21%.
P(the species is Coyote, given both clues are found) is greater than 75%.
P(at least one of the two clues is absent) equals 1 minus P(both clues are found).
P(the species is Fox, given both clues are found) is greater than P(the species is Bobcat, given both clues are found).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{both clues}) = \sum P(\text{species}) \times P(\text{print} \mid \text{species}) \times P(\text{fur} \mid \text{species})
$$

We just found $P(\text{both clues}) = 30.2\%$, which is greater than 25%.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{Co} \cap \text{both clues}) = P(\text{Co}) \times P(\text{print} \mid \text{Co}) \times P(\text{fur} \mid \text{Co})
$$

Multiply Coyote's prior by its combined likelihood of producing both clues, 0.42, found above.

$$
P(\text{Coyote} \cap \text{both clues}) = 0.50 \times 0.42 = 0.21, \text{exactly} 21\%
$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{Co} \mid \text{both clues}) =\frac{P(\text{Co} \cap \text{both clues})}{P(\text{both clues})}
$$

Divide Coyote's joint probability by the total $P(\text{both clues}) = 0.302$

$$
P(\text{Coyote} \mid \text{both clues}) =\frac{0.21}{0.302}\approx 69.5\%
$$

69.5% is not greater than 75%, so the statement is False, even though Coyote is both the most common species and has a strong combined likelihood for these two clues.

**D.** → True

The rule the claim needs is:

$$
P(\ge 1 \text{clue absent}) = 1 - P(\text{both clues present})
$$

'Both clues present' and 'at least one clue absent' are complementary, together they cover every possibility.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The claim is a comparison, so we work out both sides and line them up.

$$
\frac{P(\text{Fx} \cap \text{both})}{P(\text{both})}
$$

$$
\frac{P(\text{Bo} \cap \text{both})}{P(\text{both})}
$$

Divide each remaining joint probability by $P(\text{both clues}) = 0.302$

$$
P(\text{Fox} \mid \text{both clues}) =\frac{0.048}{0.302}\approx 15.9\%
$$

$$
P(\text{Bobcat} \mid \text{both clues}) =\frac{0.044}{0.302}\approx 14.6\%
$$

Since 15.9% is greater than 14.6%, the statement is true, though it is a close call, Fox has a much lower paw-print likelihood than Bobcat (20% vs.

55%), but a much higher fur-in-scat likelihood (80% vs.

40%), and combined with its larger prior (30% vs.

20%), it narrowly comes out ahead.

So the statement is True.

Because the paw print and the scat clue are independent of each other once the species is known, the combined likelihood of both clues together is the PRODUCT of the two individual likelihoods for each species.

$$

$$

tasks.title: A Positive Test in a Deer Population
tasks.context: In a wild deer population, 60% are Subspecies A, 25% are Subspecies B, and 15% are Subspecies C. A certain prion disease is present in 2% of Subspecies A, 6% of Subspecies B, and 15% of Subspecies C. A field test for the disease has a 90% sensitivity (probability of a positive result if the deer truly has the disease) and a 4% false-positive rate (probability of a positive result if the deer does not have the disease), regardless of subspecies. A randomly tested deer receives a POSITIVE result.
statements: P(a tested deer receives a positive result) is greater than 7%.
P(the deer is Subspecies A AND receives a positive result) is greater than 3.4%.
P(the deer is Subspecies A, given a positive result) is greater than 45%.
P(a tested deer receives a negative result) equals 1 minus P(a tested deer receives a positive result).
P(the deer is Subspecies C, given a positive result) is greater than P(the deer is Subspecies B, given a positive result).
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{positive}) = \sum P(\text{subspecies}) \times P(\text{positive} \mid \text{subspecies})
$$

We just found $P(\text{positive}) \approx 8.26\%$, which is greater than 7%.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$P(A \cap \text{positive}) = P(A) \times P(\text{positive} \mid A)$, where $P(\text{positive} \mid A)$ itself required its own Law of Total Probability

Subspecies A's joint probability was already computed above as one term of the total: $0.60 \times 0.0572 = 0.03432$ which is 3.432%, and 3.432% is indeed greater than 3.4%.

Notice this joint probability required the two-layer calculation from Step 1; you cannot get it by simply multiplying the prior by the raw disease prevalence ($0.60 \times 0.02 = 0.012$), that would ignore the test's imperfect accuracy entirely.

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(A \mid \text{positive}) =\frac{P(A \cap \text{positive})}{P(\text{positive})}
$$

Divide Subspecies A's joint probability by the total $P(\text{positive}) = 0.08257$

$$
P(A \mid \text{positive}) =\frac{0.03432}{0.08257}\approx 41.6\%
$$

41.6% is not greater than 45%, so the statement is false.

Subspecies A is the most common (60% of the population), but its low disease prevalence (2%) means most of its positive results are actually false positives from the 4% false-positive rate, not true detections, this keeps its posterior lower than the prior alone might suggest.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The rule the claim needs is:

$$
P(\text{negative}) = 1 - P(\text{positive})
$$

'Positive' and 'negative' are the only two test outcomes, so they are complementary.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The claim is a comparison, so we work out both sides and line them up.

$$
\frac{P(C \cap \text{positive})}{P(\text{positive})}
$$

$$
\frac{P(B \cap \text{positive})}{P(\text{positive})}
$$

Divide each remaining joint probability by $P(\text{positive}) = 0.08257$

$$
P(C \mid \text{positive}) =\frac{0.02535}{0.08257}\approx 30.7\%
$$

$$
P(B \mid \text{positive}) =\frac{0.0229}{0.08257}\approx 27.7\%
$$

Since 30.7% is greater than 27.7%, the statement is true, Subspecies C is both rarer and has a much higher disease prevalence (15%) than Subspecies B (6%), and that higher true-positive contribution outweighs its smaller population share.

**Note.** In every question here, the hard part is building the correct likelihood before Bayes' Theorem is even applied, squaring a single-day rate for repeated evidence (Q81), renormalizing after excluding a category (Q82), converting a success rate to a failure rate (Q83), multiplying two independent clue-likelihoods together (Q84), or running a mini Law-of- Total-Probability inside each category before running the main one across categories (Q85). Once that likelihood is correctly built, the final division step, joint probability over total probability, is exactly the same simple operation used in every earlier set.

So the statement is True.

$$

**Setup**

This question has two layers.

First, within each subspecies, we must find the chance of a POSITIVE test result, which itself depends on two things: whether the deer actually has the disease (the subspecies-specific prevalence), and whether the test result matches reality (sensitivity if diseased, false-positive rate if not diseased).

This inner calculation is its own small Law of Total Probability, run separately for each subspecies.

$$
P(\text{positive} \mid \text{subspecies}) = P(\text{disease} \mid \text{subspecies}) \times 0.90 + (1-P(\text{disease} \mid \text{subspecies})) \times 0.04
$$

Subspecies A (2% prevalence):

$$
(0.02)(0.90) + (0.98)(0.04) = 0.018 + 0.0392 = 0.0572
$$

Subspecies B (6% prevalence):

$$
(0.06)(0.90) + (0.94)(0.04) = 0.054 + 0.0376 = 0.0916
$$

Subspecies C (15% prevalence):

$$
(0.15)(0.90) + (0.85)(0.04) = 0.135 + 0.034 = 0.169
$$

Now that each subspecies has its own overall 'chance of testing positive,' treat these exactly like any other likelihood and run the usual two Bayes steps across subspecies.

$$
P(\text{positive}) = P(A)(0.0572) + P(B)(0.0916) + P(C)(0.169)
$$

$$
P(\text{positive}) = (0.60)(0.0572)+(0.25)(0.0916)+(0.15)(0.169) = 0.03432+0.0229+0.02535 = 0.08257, \text{or about} 8.26\%
$$

tasks.title: Wildfires That Escaped Containment
tasks.context: Over a 12-year monitoring period, forestry officials in a remote mountain region tracked the origin of every wildfire ignition in the area, ultimately logging 640 separate incidents across the study. Investigators found a consistent pattern in the split between causes: for every 2 wildfires traced to faulty equipment (downed power lines, sparking machinery, and the like), there were 3 ignited by lightning strikes during dry summer storms, and 5 that were ultimately attributed to human activity, such as unattended campfires or discarded cigarettes. (This 2:3:5 split describes the relative proportion of causes, not the total count of fires in any given year — the actual number of fires varied considerably from year to year depending on drought conditions and did not affect the overall proportions.) Separately, fire behavior analysts studied how often a fire escaped initial containment and grew into a large, out-of-control blaze, broken down by original cause. Records show that lightning- sparked fires spread out of control in 18 of the 300 such fires closely studied by the analysts. Human-caused fires escaped containment somewhat more often — in 40 of 500 documented cases — while equipment-caused fires, despite being the rarest category overall, proved the most dangerous once ignited, spreading out of control in 27 of just 180 studied cases. This year, a fire that dominated national headlines for weeks was confirmed, after the fact, to have spread completely out of control before firefighters could contain it.
statements: P(a wildfire spreads out of control) is greater than 8%.
P(the fire was caused by faulty equipment AND spread out of control) equals 3%.
P(the fire was caused by faulty equipment, given it spread out of control) is greater than 40%.
P(a wildfire is contained) equals 1 minus P(a wildfire spreads out of control).
P(the fire was human-caused, given it spread out of control) is greater than P(the fire was lightning-caused, given it spread out of control).

**A.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{OOC}) = \sum P(\text{cause}) \times P(\text{OOC} \mid \text{cause})
$$

We just found $P(\text{OOC}) = 8.8\%$, which is greater than 8%.

So the statement is True.

**B.** → True

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{Equip} \cap \text{OOC}) = P(\text{Equip}) \times P(\text{OOC} \mid \text{Equip})
$$

Multiply Equipment's prior (20%, from the 2:3:5 ratio) by its out-of-control rate (15%, from $\frac{27}{180}$).

$$
P(\text{Equipment} \cap \text{OOC}) = 0.20 \times 0.15 = 0.03, \text{exactly} 3\%
$$

So the statement is True.

**C.** → False

This is a Bayes' theorem question: the joint probability of the source and the evidence, divided by the total probability of the evidence.

$$
P(\text{Equip} \mid \text{OOC}) =\frac{P(\text{Equip} \cap \text{OOC})}{P(\text{OOC})}
$$

Divide Equipment's joint probability by the total $P(\text{OOC}) = 0.088$

$P(\text{Equipment} \mid \text{OOC}) =\frac{0.03}{0.088}\approx 34.1\%$, which is not greater than 40%.

Equipment-caused fires are individually the most dangerous once started (15% escape rate, the highest of the three), but they're also the rarest cause (only 20% of fires), which limits their overall share of the out-of-control cases.

So the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The rule the claim needs is:

$$
P(\text{contained}) = 1 - P(\text{OOC})
$$

'Contained' and 'out of control' are the only two outcomes for a fire, so they are complementary.

So the statement is True.

**E.** → True

The claim is a comparison, so we work out both sides and line them up.

$$
\frac{P(\text{Human} \cap \text{OOC})}{P(\text{OOC})}
$$

$$
\frac{P(\text{Lightning} \cap \text{OOC})}{P(\text{OOC})}
$$

$$
P(\text{Human} \mid \text{OOC}) =\frac{(0.50 \times 0.08)}{0.088}=\frac{0.04}{0.088}\approx 45.5\%
$$

$$
P(\text{Lightning} \mid \text{OOC}) =\frac{(0.30 \times 0.06)}{0.088}=\frac{0.018}{0.088}\approx 20.5\%
$$

Since 45.5% is greater than 20.5%, the statement is true, human-caused fires dominate the out-of-control cases mainly because they are so much more common (50% of all fires) than the other two causes, not because their individual escape rate is the highest.

tasks.title: Tagged Whales in Three Feeding Grounds
tasks.context: A marine research station has spent the last several seasons cataloguing humpback whale activity across three feeding grounds along a stretch of coastline: the Northern Strait, the Middle Channel, and the Southern Bay. Of the whales that frequent the Northern Strait, researchers have tagged 27 out of every 300 individually identified. $$
P(N \cap \text{tagged}) = P(N) \times P(\text{tagged} \mid N)
$$

Multiply Northern Strait's prior (45%) by its tagging rate (9%).

$$

$$
\frac{P(N \cap \text{tagged})}{P(\text{tagged})}
$$

$$
\frac{P(M \cap \text{tagged})}{P(\text{tagged})}
$$

$$
P(\text{Northern} \mid \text{tagged}) =\frac{0.0405}{0.109}\approx 37.2\%

$$

Since 37.2% is greater than 35.3%, the statement is true, though narrowly, Northern Strait's larger whale population (45%) just barely outweighs Middle Channel's somewhat higher tagging rate (11% vs.

9%).

So the statement is True.

tasks.title: A Genuine Meteorite in Three Search Areas
tasks.context: An amateur meteorite-hunting club has spent a decade combing three search areas after a well-documented meteor shower: a Dry Lakebed, a Rocky Plateau, and a Grassy Basin, all within the same debris field roughly 40 miles across. Club records, kept meticulously in a shared logbook since the group's founding, show that fragment discoveries are not evenly split among the three areas: for every 5 fragments found on the Rocky Plateau, members found 3 in the Dry Lakebed, and 2 in the Grassy Basin — a ratio that has stayed remarkably consistent even as the club's membership has grown from a handful of founders to well over 200 active hunters today. When fragments are sent to a university lab for verification, the confirmation rate varies noticeably by search area. Of the fragments collected from the Dry Lakebed and sent in for testing, 21 out of 300 were confirmed as genuine meteorites. Fragments from the Rocky Plateau fared better, with 60 out of 500 confirmed genuine. The Grassy Basin, though it produces the fewest total fragments of the three areas, had the highest confirmation rate: 34 out of 200 tested fragments were confirmed genuine. At this month's club meeting, a member excitedly announces that a fragment they collected this week has just come back from the lab confirmed as a genuine meteorite.
statements: P(a fragment is confirmed genuine) is greater than 10%.
P(the fragment is from the Rocky Plateau AND is confirmed genuine) equals 6%.
P(the fragment is from the Rocky Plateau, given it is confirmed genuine) is greater than 55%.
P(a fragment is not genuine) equals 1 minus P(a fragment is confirmed genuine).
P(the fragment is from the Grassy Basin, given it is confirmed genuine) is greater than P(the fragment is from the Dry Lakebed, given it is confirmed genuine).

$$

tasks.title: Mildew Across Four Vineyard Blocks
tasks.context: A family-run vineyard is laid out across four distinct blocks that climb a gentle hillside: Block A on the lower slope, Block B at mid-slope, Block C on the upper slope where the sun exposure is most intense, and Block D on the flat valley floor near a small creek. The vineyard's longtime manager, who has kept meticulous planting records since first taking over the property, reports that the blocks are not equal in size: for every 3 rows of vines in Block D, there are 4 rows in Block A, 6 rows in Block B, and 7 rows in Block C. This season, an outbreak of powdery mildew — a fungal disease that thrives in specific combinations of humidity and sun exposure — has prompted the manager to inspect a sample of rows from each block and record infection counts, separate from the routine pest-monitoring the vineyard also performs for an unrelated insect species. In Block A, inspectors found mildew in 8 of the 200 rows examined. In Block B, 27 of 300 rows examined showed signs of mildew. Block C, with its intense upper-slope sun exposure, had the highest infection count: 70 of 350 rows examined. Block D, nearest the creek and therefore more humid, still showed a meaningful rate: 21 of 150 rows examined. During today's inspection round, a randomly selected row is found to show clear signs of powdery mildew. ● (a) Find the probability that this infected row is in Block C. ● (b) Suppose the vineyard manager later confirms — from the row's marker tag — that this infected row is definitely NOT in Block C. Given both this and the fact that it is infected, find the probability that the row is in Block B.
statements: P(a row shows mildew) is greater than 10%.
P(the row is in Block C AND shows mildew) equals 7%.
P(the row is in Block C, given it shows mildew) is greater than 60%.
P(a row shows no mildew) equals 1 minus P(a row shows mildew).
P(the row is in Block B, given it shows mildew AND is known not to be in Block C) is greater than 45%.

**A.** → True

$$
